opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, USB is one of those things that's fantastic on your desk and kind of terrible inside a machine that's moving around all day. A few reasons.

First, the physical connector. USB connectors were designed for consumers plugging and unplugging things, not for vibration. There's no real positive latching on most of them, so on a robot that's driving around, bumping into things, with motors spinning, you get these micro-disconnects. The connector wiggles for a fraction of a millisecond, and from the electrical side that looks like the device went away.

And that's the second problem: the protocol's response to a glitch is really heavy. USB is a host-driven, enumerated bus. If a device drops even briefly, it doesn't just lose a packet and carry on. The host sees a disconnect, the device has to re-enumerate, the driver gets torn down and brought back up, and your application code suddenly has a file handle pointing at nothing. Maybe the camera comes back as /dev/video2 instead of /dev/video0. So a tiny physical blip turns into a multi-second outage plus a bunch of software recovery logic you now have to write and test.

Third, it's pretty sensitive to electrical noise. Inside a robot you've got motor drivers, PWM, big current swings, ground bounce, and USB at high speeds doesn't love that environment. You'll see errors that only show up when the motors are under load, which are the worst bugs to track down because everything works fine on the bench.

And then there's the hub problem. Once you have a bunch of peripherals you end up chaining hubs, and now you have shared bandwidth, shared power, and a single point of failure where one misbehaving device can take down everything downstream.

So for anything where reliability really matters, I'd much rather use something designed for that environment: CAN bus, RS-485, or Ethernet with proper locking connectors. Those are built for noisy, vibrating, industrial settings. They handle errors gracefully, a dropped frame is just a dropped frame, and there's no enumeration dance. USB is great for prototyping because everything speaks it and it's easy, but if you're building something that has to run for thousands of hours without a person babysitting it, it's one of the first things I'd design out.

r001.rationale: The response says USB connectors were designed for consumers to plug and unplug devices and describes software recovery after disconnects, but it does not attribute USB’s lower reliability standards to the assumption that a user can recover faults by unplugging and reconnecting.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to the fact that USB was never designed for the environment you have inside a robot. It was designed for someone plugging a mouse into a laptop on a desk. So the connector itself is held in mostly by friction. There's no latch, no locking mechanism, nothing positively retaining it. When you put that inside a robot that's vibrating, driving over bumps, or has a manipulator arm slamming around, those connectors slowly walk out. And the failure mode is the worst kind, because it's intermittent. The device drops off the bus for half a second, re-enumerates, maybe comes back with a different device name, and now your software is confused about which camera is which. You spend days chasing what looks like a software bug and it's actually a cable that's a millimeter loose.

The second problem is the protocol. USB is host-centric with a lot of state in the enumeration process. When something glitches, you don't get a clean error, you get a hang, or the hub resets and takes every other device down with it. In a car or an industrial setting you'd never see that, because those worlds settled on things like CAN or Ethernet with locking connectors decades ago, precisely because they'd learned these lessons. Ethernet with an RJ45 latch, or better yet an M12 connector, just doesn't have this failure mode. Same with isolated serial or CAN.

And there's the power side too. USB power delivery is negotiated, and marginal cables or hubs cause brownouts that look like random device failures. On a robot you want to control your power rails explicitly.

So my rule of thumb was, if a connection matters for the robot to keep operating, it goes on something with a positive lock and a protocol that fails loudly. USB is fine for a debug port or a dev laptop, but anything I wasn't willing to drive out to a customer site to reseat, I wouldn't put on USB.

r001.rationale: The response says USB was designed for a desk setup and describes loose connectors disconnecting and re-enumerating, but it does not attribute USB’s lower reliability standards to an assumption that a user can recover by unplugging and reconnecting devices.

astra-6.text:
USB is great for plugging a peripheral into your laptop, but inside a robot, you have vibration, electrical noise, and cables moving around. A lot of USB connectors don’t lock, so a connection can become intermittent. And an intermittent connection is much harder to debug than something that simply doesn’t work.

Then there’s recovery. If a device disconnects and reconnects, your software has to recognize that and recover gracefully. Devices sharing a hub can also affect one another, so a seemingly small failure can take out several sensors.

You can build around those problems, but for a robot that needs to run reliably, I’d prefer locking connectors and interfaces with more predictable failure and recovery behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses software recovery after a device disconnects and reconnects, but does not say USB devices have lower reliability standards because users are assumed to recover faults by unplugging and reconnecting them.

sol-6.1.text:
USB is really designed for something sitting on your desk, where if it disconnects, you unplug it and plug it back in. Inside a robot, you have vibration, electrical noise from motors, and cables moving around. Most USB connectors don’t lock, so a connection can work perfectly during testing and then become intermittent once the robot starts moving.

And the failure isn’t always clean. A device might disconnect, reset, or fail to enumerate again, and now your software has to recover from that while the robot is operating. You really want mechanically secure connectors and communication where you can detect failures and recover predictably. USB is convenient for prototyping, but that convenience can turn into a lot of debugging when you need the robot to run reliably all day.

r001.rationale: The response says USB is designed for desk use where a user can recover from a disconnect by unplugging and reconnecting it, linking that assumption to its suitability for reliability-critical robots.
